The filing says the COVID-19 pandemic contributed to a sharp decline in commercial air travel and aircraft production. Airlines delayed or canceled orders, while customers reduced inventories, lowering demand for PCC’s products. It also identifies production delays in Boeing’s 737 MAX and 787 programs as a further adverse factor for PCC’s aerospace business.

*Source: Berkshire Hathaway 2022 Form 10-K, pp. K-12 and K-49.*

ExxonMobil attributes the rise to a **tight refining market**:

- **Demand recovered:** Gasoline and diesel demand returned to pre-pandemic levels, though jet fuel demand remained below historical levels.
- **Refining capacity fell:** Shutdowns and insufficient investment, intensified by the pandemic, reduced capacity. ExxonMobil says industry rationalization took more than 3 million barrels per day offline.
- **Supply was further constrained:** Supply-chain problems and low inventories added to the tightness.

*Source: ExxonMobil 2022 Form 10-K, pp. 47, 53–54.*

As of December 31, 2023, Boeing reported these shares of its total workforce:

- **33%** — all union-represented employees, approximately 57,000 people. [Form 10-K, p. 9](BA_2023_10K.pdf#page=12)
- **21%** — represented by the International Association of Machinists and Aerospace Workers (IAM).
- **10%** — represented by the Society of Professional Engineering Employees in Aerospace (SPEEA).
- **1%** — represented by the United Automobile, Aerospace and Agricultural Implement Workers of America (UAW). [Form 10-K, p. 2](BA_2023_10K.pdf#page=5)

The three named-union percentages are included in the 33% total.

NVIDIA says these securities are investments in private companies without readily determinable fair values. Valuation is difficult because market prices, relevant market data and observable transactions are limited, the investments are inherently illiquid, and macroeconomic factors affect their value.

As a result, NVIDIA must use judgment and unobservable inputs, such as volatility, expected time to liquidity, risk-free rates, and each security’s rights and obligations. Assessing impairment also involves qualitative and quantitative factors, including the investee’s operating performance and market trends.

Source: NVIDIA fiscal 2026 Form 10-K, pp. 38, 45, 60 and 66–67.

Pfizer attributed the increase mainly to its acquisitions of Arena, Global Blood Therapeutics (GBT), and Biohaven. It provisionally recorded approximately $5.0 billion, $3.0 billion, and $450 million, respectively, in acquired IPR&D assets. [Pfizer 2022 Form 10-K, pp. 59–60, 79]

Partly offsetting the increase was a $200 million impairment of an IPR&D asset acquired with Array. The asset related to an unapproved indication for symptomatic dilated cardiomyopathy caused by a mutation in the gene encoding the lamin A/C protein. Pfizer said the impairment resulted from the Phase 3 trial reaching futility at a preplanned interim analysis. [p. 67]

Walmart reported the following long-term debt repayments for fiscal 2025, in millions of U.S. dollars:

- **$3,468 million** — total long-term debt repayments shown in the cash-flow statement and debt rollforward. (pp. 44, 57)
- **$3,373 million** — repayment of significant debt that matured during the year, comprising: (p. 69)
  - **$1,500 million** — fixed-rate debt maturing April 22, 2024.
  - **$990 million** — fixed-rate debt maturing July 8, 2024.
  - **$253 million** — yen-denominated fixed-rate debt maturing July 18, 2024.
  - **$630 million** — fixed-rate debt maturing December 15, 2024.

The $3,373 million is included in the $3,468 million total; it is not an additional repayment.

ExxonMobil’s 2025 Form 10-K reports these annual capacities for Huizhou:

- **1,600,000 metric tons:** ethylene.
- **1,700,000 metric tons:** polyethylene.
- **900,000 metric tons:** polypropylene.  
  *(Year-end 2025 capacity table, p. 21.)*

It also states that the complex’s **three polyethylene and two polypropylene lines have a combined capacity of more than 2,500,000 metric tons per year**. That combined figure covers the two polymer categories above; it is not additional capacity. *(p. 51.)*

Compared with fiscal 2025, Walmart attributed the gross profit rate increases to:

- **Company-wide, up 8 basis points:** Disciplined inventory management at Walmart U.S. and growth in higher-margin businesses globally. (p. 35)
- **Walmart U.S., up 22 basis points:** Disciplined inventory management and growth in higher-margin businesses. (p. 39)
- **Sam’s Club U.S., up 4 basis points:** Operational efficiencies and higher fuel margins. (p. 41)

Walmart International’s gross profit rate decreased, so it is not included. (p. 40)

Walmart attributed the fiscal 2025 increases in operating expenses as a percentage of net sales primarily to:

- **Company-wide:** Higher variable pay because performance exceeded plan, increased marketing, and higher depreciation expenses. The ratio rose from 20.4% to 20.7%, an increase of 36 basis points. [Form 10-K, p. 39]
- **Walmart U.S.:** The same three factors: increased marketing, higher performance-related variable pay, and increased depreciation. The ratio rose from 22.2% to 22.6%, or 44 basis points. [p. 40]
- **Sam’s Club U.S.:** Higher compensation-related expenses, including investments in associate wages and higher variable pay because performance exceeded plan, plus elevated technology spending. The ratio rose from 10.8% to 11.2%, or 44 basis points. [p. 42]

Walmart International’s ratio **fell**, rather than rose, from 18.6% to 18.5%. The displayed percentages are rounded; the basis-point changes reflect the underlying figures. [p. 41]

Boeing’s 2025 Form 10-K gives four percentages:

- **46%** of Boeing’s total 2025 revenue came from non-U.S. customers. (p. 10)
- **60%** of Commercial Airplanes’ 2025 revenue from customer contracts came from non-U.S. customers. (p. 10)
- **Approximately 85%** of Commercial Airplanes’ total backlog, by dollar value, was with non-U.S. airlines. (p. 33)
- **26%** of Defense, Space & Security’s backlog at December 31, 2025, was attributable to non-U.S. customers. (p. 38)

For the revenue figures, Boeing includes Foreign Military Sales through the U.S. government among non-U.S. customers.

### Fiscal 2025 net sales

- **40%** came through Apple’s direct distribution channels, including its stores, online stores and direct sales force.
- **60%** came through indirect channels, including third-party cellular network carriers and other resellers.  
  *Source: Apple 2025 Form 10-K, p. 2.*

### Receivables as of September 27, 2025

- **12%** of total trade receivables was attributable to one customer.
- **34%** of total trade receivables was attributable to third-party cellular network carriers collectively.
- **46% and 23%** of total vendor non-trade receivables were attributable to two manufacturing vendors, respectively. These receivables arose from Apple’s sales of components to those vendors.  
  *Source: Apple 2025 Form 10-K, p. 39.*

Apple identified the following results as adversely affected by currency weakness against the U.S. dollar:

| Result | Fiscal 2024 | Fiscal 2023 | Currency effect |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| Greater China net sales | $66.952 billion | $72.559 billion | Weaker renminbi |
| Japan net sales | $25.052 billion | $24.257 billion | Weaker yen |
| Rest of Asia Pacific net sales | $30.658 billion | $29.615 billion | Net effect of weaker foreign currencies |
| Products gross margin | $109.633 billion | $108.803 billion | Weaker foreign currencies |
| Products gross margin percentage | 37.2% | 36.5% | Weaker foreign currencies |

For both Products gross margin measures, currency weakness and a different product mix **partially offset** cost savings. Apple did not quantify the separate currency impact in these explanations.

Source: Apple fiscal 2024 Form 10-K, pp. 22 and 24.

Boeing’s 2022 filing reports these fixed-price revenue shares:

- **Commercial Airplanes (BCA): 100%**
- **Defense, Space & Security (BDS): 60%**
- **Global Services (BGS), overall: 88%**
- **BGS’s defense business specifically: approximately 69%**

The 69% figure applies only to BGS’s defense business, not the entire BGS segment.

Source: Boeing 2022 Form 10-K, pp. 13 and 111–112.

ExxonMobil’s 2025 Form 10-K gives four quantified annual sensitivities:

| Change | Stated annual effect |
|---|---:|
| **Brent crude:** $1 per barrel | Approximately **$700 million** effect on Upstream earnings |
| **Henry Hub natural gas:** $0.10 per million British thermal units | Approximately **$90 million** effect on Upstream earnings |
| **Title Transfer Facility (TTF) natural gas:** $0.10 per million British thermal units | Approximately **$20 million** effect on Upstream earnings |
| **Pension accounting:** 0.5-percentage-point reduction in the assumed long-term return on assets worldwide | Approximately **$150 million increase** in pension expense |

The commodity-price sensitivities are estimates for **2026**, after tax, for consolidated and equity-company Upstream earnings, excluding derivatives. ExxonMobil cautions that benchmark price changes are only broad indicators of actual earnings effects. The pension-expense estimate is **before tax**. (Form 10-K, printed pp. 62 and 67; PDF pp. 64 and 69.)

Pfizer’s 2024 Form 10-K gives the following Haleon ownership figures:

| Point in time | Pfizer’s ownership |
|---|---:|
| December 31, 2023 | 32% |
| After the March 2024 sale | Approximately 23% |
| December 31, 2024, after the October sale | Approximately 15% |
| After an additional sale in the first quarter of 2025 | Approximately 7% |

The filing also says Pfizer sold approximately **30% and 34% of its then-held investment** in March and October 2024, respectively. Those figures describe portions of Pfizer’s holdings sold, not its ownership of Haleon.

Source: Pfizer 2024 Form 10-K, Note 2C, p. 66, and MD&A, p. 47.

NVIDIA’s fiscal 2023 Form 10-K reports these effects:

- **Blocked products and support:** Sanctions and export controls imposed in response to the war blocked NVIDIA’s products, services and support from entering Russia, Belarus and certain regions of Ukraine. (p. 28)
- **Russian operations:** NVIDIA stopped direct sales to Russia during fiscal 2023 and later closed its business operations there. It said direct sales to Russia in fiscal 2022 had been immaterial. (pp. 28, 37)
- **Sales and revenue:** The war affected end-customer sales in Europe, the Middle East and Africa. NVIDIA also said its revenue from partners selling into Russia **may have been negatively affected** by the war. (pp. 28, 37)

- **Clayton Homes:** Affiliate borrowings increased **$6.6 billion** during 2024, reaching **$24.3 billion** at December 31. The borrowings largely funded its home-loan portfolio. [2024 Form 10-K, p. K-48]
- **Pilot Travel Centers:** Borrowed **$5.7 billion** from Berkshire insurance subsidiaries in March 2024 to repay third-party debt, then repaid **$1.0 billion** of the affiliate borrowings during the year. [2024 Form 10-K, p. K-53]

As of January 31, 2026, Walmart reported:

- **$6,020 million** in notional amount for the cross-currency swaps designated as cash-flow hedges. The notional amount is a reference for contractual payments, not the swaps’ fair value. (p. 69)
- **$(920) million** in fair value—a liability. The market-risk discussion reports the same aggregate liability, rounded, as **$0.9 billion**. (pp. 47, 69)
- **$0.7 billion** in hypothetical change in swap value from a uniform 10% weakening of the U.S. dollar against the currencies underlying the swaps. (p. 47)
- **$0.1 billion** in hypothetical change in swap value from a 10% change in the underlying interest rates from their January 31, 2026 market rates. (p. 47)

The last two amounts are sensitivities, not additional reported liabilities. Source: *Walmart fiscal 2026 Form 10-K*.

The filing says the initial effects of COVID-19 on commercial airlines and aircraft manufacturers were particularly severe. In reassessing PCC, Berkshire considered airlines’ announcements about future demand, employment levels and aircraft orders; manufacturers’ announced production cuts; and restructuring actions Berkshire was taking or might take.

Given the risks and uncertainties facing the aerospace industry, Berkshire increased the discount rates and reduced its long-term cash-flow forecasts used to estimate fair values. The resulting impairment reviews identified carrying values above estimated fair values. Berkshire noted that these valuations required significant judgment and that actual results could differ substantially from forecasts.

*Source: Berkshire Hathaway 2021 Form 10-K, pp. K-62–K-63 and K-89.*

**Balances at January 25, 2026**

- **$20.832 billion:** Total goodwill on NVIDIA’s consolidated balance sheet, rounded to $20.8 billion in Note 5.
- **$20.5 billion:** Goodwill allocated to the Compute & Networking reporting unit.
- **$370 million:** Goodwill allocated to the Graphics reporting unit. The reporting-unit figures are rounded.  
  *(Form 10-K, pp. 53, 63)*

**Goodwill added during fiscal 2026**

- **$15.6 billion:** The overall increase in goodwill, allocated to Compute & Networking.
- **$14.4 billion:** Goodwill recorded for the Groq technology-license and employee-hiring arrangement. It was primarily attributable to the workforce and future development of the licensed technology, and is tax-deductible. *(pp. 61, 63)*

The Groq amount is included in the overall increase and the Compute & Networking balance; it is not additional to them.

- **Employees:** IAM District 837 represented approximately **3,200 Boeing employees** at St. Louis-area sites. The filing gives this as the number represented, not a separate count of employees who struck. (p. 2)
- **Strike:** The work stoppage began **August 4, 2025**, and lasted **101 days**. It ended when employees voted to ratify a new contract on **November 13, 2025**. (pp. 2, 24)
- **Agreement:** Boeing lists the principal District 837 agreement’s location as Missouri and its expiration as **July 2030**. The filing does not give an exact expiration day or state the agreement’s term length. (p. 2)

Source: Boeing, 2025 Form 10-K.

An improved macroeconomic environment supported consumer credit performance. Elevated consumer cash balances contributed to lower credit card charge-offs and higher recoveries, and to lower auto charge-offs alongside higher vehicle collateral values. Residential real estate recoveries increased as home prices improved and low interest rates led to prepayments and more reversals of prior write-downs. (2021 Form 10-K, pp. 110, 113–114, 116.)

Growth in balances in new and existing client accounts, reflecting higher-yielding product offerings; and the full-year effect of First Republic–associated deposits transferred to Asset & Wealth Management in the fourth quarter of 2023. (2024 Form 10-K, pp. 84, 111)

The filing cites production losses from:

- **Divestments** of assets.
- **Russia’s expropriation** of ExxonMobil’s Sakhalin-1 interests.
- **Other impacts**, including weather-related downtime.

In its production-volume reconciliation, it also cites **lower entitlements due to higher prices**. [ExxonMobil 2022 Form 10-K, pp. 48, 50, 52; PDF pp. 50, 52, 54.]

Walmart’s fiscal 2022 Form 10-K reports these counts **as of January 31, 2022**:

| Business segment | Pickup | Delivery |
|---|---:|---:|
| Walmart U.S. | **Approximately 4,600** pickup locations | **More than 3,500** same-day delivery locations |
| Walmart International | **Approximately 2,900** pickup locations | **Over 1,900** delivery locations |

The International count is for delivery generally; the filing does not characterize the entire count as same-day delivery. (Form 10-K, pp. 7, 9.)

Separately, **Sam’s Club** says Curbside Pickup was available at **all clubs**; the filing lists **600 clubs** in the U.S. and Puerto Rico. It describes delivery-from-club but gives no delivery-location count in that segment description. (pp. 10, 27.)

- Growth in credit-card loans, reflecting new accounts and revolving balances. (2025 Form 10-K, p. 117)
- Higher commercial and industrial charge-offs, including in technology, media and telecommunications, and healthcare. (p. 124)
- Estimated losses from borrower fraud in certain secured lending facilities. (p. 124)
- A third-quarter charge-off on a client-specific exposure in Asset & Wealth Management. (p. 76)

Pfizer reported the following Upjohn separation costs:

- **Approximately $700 million** in expected total costs, including legal-entity separation expenses and transaction costs.
- **Approximately 75%** of that expected total had been incurred from inception through December 31, 2021. (Form 10-K, p. 26)
- **$434 million in 2020** and **$83 million in 2019** in separation-related costs incurred in those respective years. These were included in “Discontinued operations—net of tax” and primarily covered professional fees for regulatory filings and separation activities, as well as investment banking fees. (Note 2B, p. 65)

The annual amounts are incurred costs, not amounts to add to the overall estimate.

The filing identifies four dates or months in 2025:

- **April 23 — EU Digital Markets Act investigations.** The European Commission fined Apple **€500 million** in its Article 5(4) investigation and ordered it to remove restrictions preventing developers from steering users to alternative distribution channels outside the App Store. Apple appealed. The same day, the Commission issued preliminary findings in a separate Article 6(4) investigation into Apple’s contractual requirements for third-party developers and app marketplaces. [Form 10-K, p. 18; PDF p. 21]

- **April 30 — Epic Games litigation.** The California district court found Apple had violated its 2021 injunction and barred, among other things, commissions or fees on purchases consumers make outside an app. It also denied Apple’s motion to narrow or vacate the injunction and referred Apple to the U.S. Attorney for possible criminal contempt proceedings. [p. 18; PDF p. 21]

- **September 2 — Google antitrust case.** Following a 2024 finding that Google violated U.S. antitrust law, the D.C. district court ordered certain remedies. The filing does not detail those remedies; it says further proceedings or appeals could change them. It warns that a previously proposed restriction on Google’s search-distribution commercial terms, if imposed, could affect Apple’s licensing revenue. [p. 14; PDF p. 17]

- **October 2025 — Epic Games appeal.** The Ninth Circuit heard oral arguments on Apple’s expedited appeal of the April ruling. The filing gives the month, not the day. [p. 18; PDF p. 21]

Pfizer attributed the favorable change primarily to a swing from **net losses on equity securities of $1.273 billion in 2022 to net gains of $1.590 billion in 2023**, and to lower net interest expense. The 2023 gains included a $1.7 billion realized gain on Telavant and a $297 million unrealized gain on Cerevel, partly offset by a $292 million unrealized loss on BioNTech.

Partly offsetting those favorable factors were higher intangible-asset impairment charges: approximately $3.0 billion in 2023, compared with $421 million in 2022. The 2023 charges included $1.4 billion for etrasimod following changes in development plans and revenue expectations, and $964 million for Prevnar 13 following updated commercial forecasts.

Net interest expense fell from $987 million to $585 million. Interest expense rose, driven by $31 billion of notes Pfizer issued in May 2023 to help finance its Seagen acquisition. That increase was more than offset by higher interest income from investing the debt issuance’s net proceeds: total interest income rose from $251 million to $1.624 billion.

*Source: Pfizer 2023 Form 10-K, p. 40 and Note 4, p. 73.*

NVIDIA’s fiscal 2024 Form 10-K disclosed:

- **$2.2 billion** in total provisions for inventory and excess inventory purchase obligations. (p. 40)
- **$774 million** in inventory provisions charged to cost of revenue. (Note 10, p. 68)
- **Approximately $1.4 billion** in cost-of-revenue expense for inventory purchase obligations above current demand projections, supplier charges, and cancellation and underutilization penalties. (Note 10, p. 70)
- **$540 million** in provision releases from sales of previously reserved inventory or settlements of excess inventory purchase obligations. (p. 40)

The $774 million and approximately $1.4 billion figures are components of the reported total, not additional charges. The releases reduce the net effect.

The adoption increased the following previously reported earnings measures, in **millions of dollars**:

| Earnings measure | 2021 change | 2022 change |
|---|---:|---:|
| Berkshire Hathaway Reinsurance Group pre-tax underwriting earnings | +$175 | +$76 |
| Insurance underwriting earnings, after tax | +$142 | +$60 |
| Net earnings attributable to Berkshire Hathaway shareholders | +$142 | +$60 |

A positive change means higher earnings or a smaller loss. These measures overlap, so the changes should not be added together.

Source: Berkshire Hathaway 2023 Form 10-K, pp. K-35, K-39 and K-82.

Two filings state a remaining transition-tax amount:

| Company | Total remaining at fiscal 2021 year-end |
|---|---:|
| Apple | **$24.6 billion** |
| Pfizer | **$8.3 billion**, estimated |

Apple said none of its balance was payable within the next 12 months. Pfizer estimated that $750 million of its total would be paid within 12 months. Sources: Apple’s 2021 Form 10-K, p. 25; Pfizer’s 2021 Form 10-K, p. 47.

The JPMorgan Chase, Berkshire Hathaway, ExxonMobil and Boeing filings do not separately state an identifiable year-end balance for this tax. That does not necessarily mean they owed nothing.

Pfizer attributes the increase primarily to approximately $8.0 billion of IPR&D it provisionally recorded upon acquiring Metsera, a clinical-stage company developing obesity and cardiometabolic medicines. The increase was partly offset by $3.9 billion in IPR&D impairments and transfers from IPR&D to developed-technology rights of $600 million for Padcev and $590 million for talazoparib (Talzenna). (2025 Form 10-K, Notes 2A and 10, pp. 64 and 83.)

Pfizer says the impairments were primarily due to **changes in development plans and updated long-range commercial forecasts**. The $3.9 billion included approximately $1.6 billion for disitamab vedotin, $820 million for Tukysa (tucatinib), and $820 million for osivelotor. Pfizer does not give a separate reason for each charge in that disclosure. (Note 4, p. 70.)

Walmart’s fiscal 2022 Form 10-K gives these Flipkart-related figures:

- **$3.2 billion:** Walmart received this amount in fiscal 2022 from subsidiary stock sales, **primarily** related to new equity funding for Flipkart. That funding reduced Walmart’s ownership from approximately **83%** at January 31, 2021 to approximately **75%**. [pp. 43, 64; Exhibit 21, p. 164]
- **$2.2 billion:** Cash at January 31, 2022 that Walmart could access only through dividends or intercompany financing arrangements subject to Flipkart minority-shareholder approval. Walmart expected Flipkart to use the cash. [p. 42]
- **$0.4 billion:** Fiscal 2020 impairment charges in Walmart International consisting **primarily** of writing off the carrying value of Flipkart’s Jabong.com fashion trade name, following a decision to focus on Myntra.com. [p. 71]

Source: *Walmart Inc. fiscal 2022 Form 10-K*.

As of December 31, 2022, Boeing reported **$794 million** of capitalized precontract costs in inventory. [Form 10-K, p. 76](BA_2022_10K.pdf#page=80)

The filing also identified these program-specific amounts:

| Amount ($ millions) | Related to |
|---:|---|
| Approximately **209** | KC-46A Tanker unexercised future production lots |
| Approximately **180** | Commercial Crew unauthorized future missions |
| Approximately **56** | T-7A Red Hawk future production lots |

These amounts are included in the $794 million total; they do not account for all of it. [Form 10-K, pp. 87–88](BA_2022_10K.pdf#page=91)

JPMorgan adopted the TDR guidance using the **modified retrospective method**. The reported adoption effects, in millions of dollars, were:

| Measure | Effect | What it represents |
|---|---:|---|
| Firmwide allowance for credit losses | **−$587** | The net adoption-date decrease. The same $587 is reported as a decrease in the allowance for loan losses; it is not a second reduction. |
| Consumer loans excluding credit cards | **−$489** | The adoption effect on that portfolio’s allowance for loan losses. |
| Credit card loans | **−$100** | The adoption effect on the credit card allowance for loan losses. |
| Wholesale loans | **+$2** | The adoption effect on the wholesale allowance for loan losses, partly offsetting the consumer reductions. |
| Consumer & Community Banking | **−$591** | The segment’s net decrease in its allowance for loan losses, driven by residential real estate and credit cards. This overlaps the firmwide and portfolio amounts above. |
| Retained earnings | **+$446** | The firmwide cumulative adoption adjustment, **after tax**. |

The portfolio amounts reconcile to the $587 million firmwide loan-loss allowance decrease. Sources: [2023 Form 10-K, pp. 70, 173 and 258](JPM_2023_10K.pdf).

The consolidated equity statement also shows a **$449 million** cumulative increase in retained earnings, but that figure relates to *both* the TDR guidance and a separate hedging-accounting change; it is not the TDR effect alone. [2023 Form 10-K, p. 169](JPM_2023_10K.pdf).

Berkshire attributed the following **pre-tax losses** to Hurricane Ian:

| Insurance operation or total | Amount | Filing reference |
|---|---:|---|
| GEICO: losses and loss adjustment expenses | Approximately **$400 million** | p. K-36 |
| Berkshire Hathaway Primary Group: incurred losses | **$554 million** | p. K-37 |
| Berkshire Hathaway Reinsurance Group: property/casualty incurred losses | **$1.6 billion** | p. K-38 |
| Consolidated current-accident-year incurred losses | Approximately **$2.5 billion** | p. K-92 |

The consolidated figure is **not an additional loss** to add to the operation-level amounts. The filing states the consolidated incurred losses net of reinsurance recoveries.

**Three filings** identify a group acting collectively as the chief operating decision maker (CODM):

- **JPMorgan Chase:** the **Operating Committee**. Its members act collectively as the CODM. *(2024 Form 10-K, Note 32, PDF p. 315.)*
- **Berkshire Hathaway:** an **unnamed group** comprising the chairman and CEO, the vice chairman of insurance operations, and the vice chairman of non-insurance operations. *(Note 26, PDF p. 110.)*
- **ExxonMobil:** the **Management Committee**, comprising the CEO, CFO and two senior vice presidents overseeing the Upstream and Product Solutions businesses. *(Note 18, PDF p. 110.)*

NVIDIA, Pfizer and Boeing identify their CEO as the CODM. Apple and Walmart refer to a CODM in their fiscal 2024 segment notes but do not identify who fills that role. *(NVIDIA, PDF p. 78; Pfizer, p. 111; Boeing, p. 118; Apple, p. 49; Walmart, p. 78.)*

Apple identifies several influences on quarterly net sales:

- **Holiday demand:** Sales have historically been higher in the first fiscal quarter, partly because of seasonal holiday demand. (p. 4)
- **Product and service launches:** Introductions can significantly affect sales. Consumers and distributors may respond in anticipation of a launch; inventories of older products often decline beforehand, while indirect channels are stocked with new products afterward. (p. 4)
- **Dependence on one product:** A decline in demand for a product that accounts for a significant share of sales could substantially affect a quarter. In fiscal 2023, iPhone represented about 52% of Apple’s total net sales. (pp. 15, 22)
- **Unexpected developments:** These include lower-than-anticipated demand, problems with introductions, IT or network disruptions, and failures of logistics, component-supply or manufacturing partners. (p. 15)

For comparison purposes, Apple also notes that its first fiscal quarter contains an extra week every five or six years; fiscal 2023 was one such year. (p. 20)

**Five filings** report qualifying repurchases during fiscal 2025:

| Company | Shares repurchased (millions) | Source, PDF page |
|---|---:|---|
| NVIDIA | 310 | `NVDA_2025_10K.pdf`, p. 33 |
| Apple | 402 | `AAPL_2025_10K.pdf`, p. 47 |
| Walmart | 61.9 | `WMT_2025_10K.pdf`, p. 67 |
| JPMorgan Chase | 114.4 | `JPM_2025_10K.pdf`, p. 99 |
| ExxonMobil | 180.1 | `XOM_2025_10K.pdf`, p. 62 |

Walmart’s figure is on a settlement-date basis. NVIDIA’s count reflects its stock split and excludes purchases after its fiscal year ended.

**The other three do not qualify:**

- **Berkshire Hathaway:** No shares were repurchased in 2025. (`BRK_2025_10K.pdf`, p. 57)
- **Pfizer:** No shares were purchased under its publicly announced plan. Its reported fourth-quarter purchases were tax-withholding shares or trustee purchases. (`PFE_2025_10K.pdf`, pp. 37, 101)
- **Boeing:** Its repurchase program ended in 2020; the shares transferred to it in 2025 were for employee tax withholding. (`BA_2025_10K.pdf`, pp. 25, 45)

Boeing reported the following **787-only abnormal production costs**:

- **$468 million:** Costs expensed in 2021. (pp. 29, 77)
- **$1,240 million:** Costs expensed in 2022. (pp. 29, 77)
- **$1.7 billion:** Cumulative abnormal costs recorded through December 31, 2022. (p. 33)
- **$2.8 billion:** Boeing’s revised estimate of total cumulative abnormal production costs, made in the fourth quarter of 2022. It expected most to be incurred by the end of 2023. (p. 33)
- **Approximately $2 billion:** The earlier estimate of total cumulative abnormal production costs, as of December 31, 2021. (p. 33)

These amounts overlap: the annual expenses are part of the cumulative amount, and the two estimates are alternative forecasts of total costs, not additional costs. Boeing attributed abnormal costs to low production rates and excessive inspections and rework. (p. 33)

The Form 10-K reports these transfers to Corporate in the first quarter of 2025:

- **419 employees** from Consumer & Community Banking.
- **219 employees** from Commercial & Investment Bank.
- **130 employees** from Asset & Wealth Management.
- **768 employees in total** from the lines of business—the sum of the three figures above, not an additional transfer.

Source: JPMorgan Chase & Co., *2025 Form 10-K*, pp. 67, 72, 77–78 and 80.

The 10-K explicitly says three projects were **funded in 2021**:

- **Bacalhau Phase 1, Brazil:** ExxonMobil also says it announced the final investment decision in June 2021. (Form 10-K pp. 16 and 46; PDF pp. 18 and 48.)
- **North Field Production Sustainment Integrated Drilling and Looping, Qatar.** (p. 17; PDF p. 19.)

### Financial results and cash flow

- **Gain:** The exchange produced an initial **$7.990 billion gain** based on the fair value of the Class C shares. Class C fair-value changes, derivative-value changes and dividends brought the **net Visa-related gain recorded in the second quarter to $7.9 billion**. The initial gain is part of that net figure, not additional to it. The gain was reported in Corporate and increased noninterest revenue. (pp. 54, 88, 200, 228)
- **Foundation contribution:** The Firm recorded **$1.0 billion of noninterest expense** in the second quarter for Class C shares contributed to the JPMorgan Chase Foundation. The other Class C shares were sold in the second and third quarters; none remained by September 30. The reported second-quarter gain and contribution imply roughly **$6.9 billion of pretax benefit** for that quarter. (pp. 54, 62, 200, 228)
- **Cash-flow reconciliation:** The statement of cash flows subtracts the **$7.990 billion initial exchange gain** from net income in reconciling operating cash flow. This is a reconciliation adjustment, not a second loss. (p. 176)
- **Taxes:** The Visa gain and contribution were among the factors affecting the Firm’s higher effective tax rate: **22.1% in 2024 versus 19.6% in 2023**. The filing does not isolate a Visa-specific tax amount. (p. 62)

### Risk measures and remaining exposure

Holding Class C shares elevated the **average and maximum** Corporate, Other and Total risk-management value-at-risk (VaR). The filing reports these one-day, approximately 95%-confidence measures in millions: (pp. 143–144)

| VaR measure | 2024 average / maximum | 2023 average / maximum |
|---|---:|---:|
| Corporate | $23 / $102 | $12 / $17 |
| Other | $25 / $101 | $14 / $22 |
| Total | $47 / $91 | $43 / $57 |

Average Total VaR rose **$4 million** year over year, but that change was not solely attributable to Visa: purchased credit protection also increased VaR, partly offset by older fixed-income volatility leaving the historical look-back period. The second-quarter rise and subsequent decline in daily VaR primarily reflected changes in Class C exposure.

The Firm retained **18.6 million Class B-2 shares** at a nominal carryover basis. Their transfer restrictions and ultimate conversion rate remained uncertain pending litigation; the stated year-end rate was **1.5430 Class A shares per B-2 share**. The shares fell within the measurement-alternative category excluded from the Firm’s other debt-and-equity sensitivity measure. Separately, derivatives associated with **11.6 million B-2 shares** from pre-2024 Visa share sales continued to expose the Firm to conversion-rate changes; their notional had been adjusted for the exchange.
